# CRW-1058: GNU parallel templates and pipe- or descriptor-fed programs. {MEMORY} the protected memory root, {CHECKOUT} the managed
# checkout. The harmless shapes are controls (B); each protected shape keeps the refusal its consumer gives (W, P, R); a shape the reader
# cannot prove stays U.

=== CRW-1058-01 | B
--why parallel with a plain echo template: the expanded lines are echo commands that touch no gate.
--cmd
parallel echo {} ::: a b

=== CRW-1058-02 | B
--why parallel options that change no command line (-j, -k), a path modifier and the sequence number.
--cmd
parallel -j2 -k echo {/.} {#} ::: dir/a.tar.gz other/b.txt

=== CRW-1058-03 | B
--why linked sources (:::+) and two sources named by position: the expanded lines are echo commands.
--cmd
parallel echo {1} {2} ::: a b :::+ c d

=== CRW-1058-04 | B
--why printf writes a literal echo line; the shell runs it: echo, touches no gate.
--cmd
printf 'echo hi\n' | bash

=== CRW-1058-05 | B
--why echo writes a literal text into a shell with a dash option: the bytes are the program.
--cmd
echo 'echo hi' | sh -s

=== CRW-1058-06 | B
--why a descriptor 3 holds a here-document with an echo: bash runs the body, which touches no gate.
--cmd
bash /dev/fd/3 3<<'EOF'
echo hi
EOF

=== CRW-1058-07 | B
--why the here-string form of the same descriptor shape.
--cmd
bash /dev/fd/3 3<<<'echo hi'

=== CRW-1058-08 | B
--why a python program on a copied descriptor: print touches no gate.
--cmd
python3 /dev/fd/4 3<<'PY' 4<&3
print(1)
PY

=== CRW-1058-09 | W
--why parallel's expanded cp writes into the memory root: the destination is the template's {MEMORY} with the source value.
--cmd
parallel cp /tmp/x {MEMORY}/{} ::: a

=== CRW-1058-10 | W
--why a literal printf carries an echo redirected into the memory root: the shell runs it.
--cmd
printf 'echo x > {MEMORY}/a' | bash

=== CRW-1058-11 | W
--why the same redirect on a descriptor copied from a here-document.
--cmd
bash /dev/fd/3 3<<'EOF'
echo x > {MEMORY}/a
EOF

=== CRW-1058-12 | W
--why parallel's template word joins a redirect into the memory root: the expanded line writes there.
--cmd
parallel echo x '>' {MEMORY}/{} ::: a

=== CRW-1058-13 | P
--why a literal printf carries a GitHub comment: the post guard refuses an inline body carried by a shell.
--cmd
printf 'gh pr comment 1 -b plain' | bash

=== CRW-1058-14 | P
--why parallel expands a GitHub comment with an inline body: the post guard refuses it.
--cmd
parallel gh pr comment {} -b plain ::: 1

=== CRW-1058-15 | R
--why parallel's expanded rm removes the managed checkout named by its source.
--cmd
parallel rm -rf {} ::: {CHECKOUT}

=== CRW-1058-16 | R
--why a literal printf carries the removal of the managed checkout.
--cmd
printf 'rm -rf {CHECKOUT}' | bash

=== CRW-1058-17 | R
--why a descriptor copied from a here-document carries the removal of the managed checkout.
--cmd
bash /dev/fd/3 3<<'EOF'
rm -rf {CHECKOUT}
EOF

=== CRW-1058-18 | U
--why a parallel source the reader cannot see: the expanded commands are unknown.
--cmd
parallel rm -rf {} ::: $X

=== CRW-1058-19 | U
--why a pipe whose producer word is unknown: the program bytes are not shown.
--cmd
printf "$X" | bash

=== CRW-1058-20 | U
--why a parallel template run on a remote host: the program runs elsewhere, not in the text.
--cmd
parallel -S host rm -rf {} ::: {CHECKOUT}

=== CRW-1058-21 | U
--why parallel reads its sources from a file: the removal targets are not in the text.
--cmd
parallel rm -rf {} :::: list.txt

=== CRW-1058-22 | U
--why a pipe the shell reads with its own stdin redirection stays refused (zsh MULTIOS reads the pipe and the file).
--cmd
printf 'rm -rf {CHECKOUT}' | bash </dev/null

=== CRW-1058-23 | U
--why a descriptor alias the text never sets: no program is shown.
--cmd
bash /dev/fd/3

=== CRW-1058-24 | B
--why bash -s reads its program from the pipe; the operand foo is a positional parameter, not a script file. The program is echo.
--cmd
printf 'echo hi\n' | bash -s foo

=== CRW-1058-25 | R
--why bash -s with an operand: the piped removal is the program the shell runs, not the script file named by the operand.
--cmd
printf 'rm -rf {CHECKOUT}' | bash -s foo

=== CRW-1058-26 | U
--why echo takes a repeated -n and bash also takes -e and -E as options: the rm the text hides behind the -e word is what the shell runs, so the program is unreadable.
--cmd
echo -n -e 'rm -rf {CHECKOUT}' | bash

=== CRW-1058-27 | B
--why a repeated -n is still an echo option: the piped text is echo hi, which touches no gate.
--cmd
echo -n -n 'echo hi' | bash

=== CRW-1058-28 | U
--why a function named echo runs in place of the echo the pipe producer names: the function prints the removal, so the program is unreadable.
--cmd
echo() { printf 'rm -rf {CHECKOUT}'; }; echo ignored | bash

=== CRW-1058-29 | attempt/allow/deny
--why bash - reads its operand as a script file, as bash -- does: remove.sh holds the removal (the worktree guard refuses it), and the memory gate asks a grant for a script it cannot see into.
--file remove.sh
rm -rf {CHECKOUT}
--cmd
bash - remove.sh <<<':'

=== CRW-1058-30 | U
--why a here-string on the shell's own input replaces the pipe for bash and is read with it by zsh (MULTIOS): the program is unreadable.
--cmd
printf 'rm -rf {CHECKOUT}\n' | bash /dev/stdin <<<'echo hi'

=== CRW-1058-31 | R
--why parallel runs each job in its own shell from the directory of the text: the second job removes ../repo from the checkout itself, and the cd of the first job does not reach it.
--cmd
parallel -j1 cd '{}' ';' rm -rf ../repo ::: sub .

=== CRW-1058-32 | R
--why {.} removes the extension from the final path component only: the dotted parent stays, so the value names the checkout.
--cmd
parallel rm -rf '{.}' ::: ../repo.v1/../repo

=== CRW-1058-33 | U
--why an xargs operand is one more ::: source of parallel: the checkout path xargs appends is a value the reader cannot see, so the program is unreadable.
--cmd
echo {CHECKOUT} | xargs parallel rm -rf '{}' ::: /tmp/unprotected

=== CRW-1058-34 | B
--why a literal pipe program whose shell sends its own standard output to /dev/null: the piped echo is the program, and it touches no gate.
--cmd
printf 'echo hi\n' | bash >/dev/null

=== CRW-1058-35 | B
--why a descriptor 0 copied from a here-string on descriptor 3: the body that descriptor holds is echo hi, which touches no gate.
--cmd
bash /dev/stdin 3<<<'echo hi' 0<&3

=== CRW-1058-36 | B
--why the same copy read by python: the here-string on descriptor 3 is print(1), which touches no gate.
--cmd
python3 /dev/fd/0 3<<<'print(1)' 0<&3
